So I'd rather not go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I have finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now please have P2532 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, just for your information, the document coming up on your screen comes from a notebook kept by Ratko Mladic. And the entry that we are looking at is from 13 December 1993, although that's not what's on our screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: It says July 1994, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr will find the right pages, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I think what we need is P2532.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So this comes from a notebook kept by Ratko Mladic, and this entry is from the 13th of December, 1993. So this is still about three months before your arrival in Belgrade. It is just around the time of your meeting with Lord Owen that you described during your direct exam. And this records a meeting in Belgrade attended by two delegation: One is from Serbia and one is from the RS. From Serbia the attendees were: Milosevic, General Perisic, Sokolovic, Stanisic, Badza, Tepavcevic, and General Mrksic. From the RS the attendees were Karadzic, Krajisnik, Mladic, Milovanovic, Cukic, Miletic, Maric, Salapura, Stanisic, and Kovac. Jovica Stanisic speaks first at the meeting, and he says: "It is because of your initiative that we are meeting in order to improve your operational and tactical position and see about help from Serbia." Karadzic speaks next, and he says: "We are moving towards the end of the conflict. This moment is the most favourable for us to end the war. We are holding 75 per cent of the territory and controlling the most important parts of the territory." Are you able to confirm at the time of your arrival in Belgrade in March 1994 that Bosnian Serbs were controlling about 75 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: I would have thought the figure was slightly less, maybe 68, 70 per cent, I can't quite remember. Seventy-five per cent seems rather high, but I mean, I'm not saying it's wrong. It just doesn't seem what my memory tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Karadzic continues saying: "We have not achieved some of it in the Neretva valley and a foothold on the coast which we could have achieve by political means. "We have to return part of the territory because the MZ or international community will not agree to 31 per cent of the Serbs holding 75 per cent of the territory. "Unification with Serbia is smiling upon us." Now Mr. Karadzic is also correct here when he says that the international community was not willing to let the Bosnian Serbs keep 75 per cent of the territory of Bosnia. And, in fact, the exchange of territory for official recognition of the Republika Srpska was one of the key issues in the contact group plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And then moving on to the bottom of the page, Karadzic says: "What are our strategy objectives? "1. To be separated from the Muslims and Croats. "2. To establish territorial control in Posavina. "3. For the Drina not to be the border. "4. To take control of part of the Neretva valley. "5. To have a foothold on the coast. "6. To have our part of Sarajevo." Were you aware of these six strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs and that they were published in the Official Gazette of the RS in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, is there any dispute about the strategic objectives or -- because it comes a bit as a surprise in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has knowledge of them. It may be relevant for his evidence about the negotiations or about the goals of the contact group plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But apparently he is not aware of them. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me add that I wasn't aware of them as set out some two years before I arrived. But it was quite clear that objective 1, 2, 4 -- sorry, 5 and 6 were things that the Bosnian Serbs always went on about. I take it that 3, for the Drina not to be the border, refers back to the line that you quoted two lines above, unification with Serbia is smiling upon us; i.e., that the Drina should not be a border between Republika Srpska and Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are you in a position to comment on the extent to which any of these goals had been achieved in Bosnia by the time you arrived in Belgrade in March of 1994?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to make such categorical statements, to be separated from the Muslims and Croats? Well, they were fighting each other in two different camps, as it were. Territorial control in Posavina, that was being fought over; for the Drina not to be the border, well, that's -- that was something that was never achieved; the Neretva valley, I don't remember; have a foothold on the coast, no, they never achieved that; to have their part of the Sarajevo, well they had their part of Sarajevo and were bombing rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What follows in this meeting is a discussion of two potential military operations; one at various elevations around Sarajevo, including one called mount Zuc, and one in the Praca river valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could have the bottom of page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to read Milosevic's conclusions. He says: "1. Do not plan and do not do Praca. "2. Work out the Sarajevo operation. "3. The SRK does not have its own forces. They have to resolve this quickly and with assistance." And, sir, just so you know, it's our case that SRK is the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the VRS Corps engaged in the siege of Sarajevo: "4. How to neutralise propaganda around Sarajevo ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could have the next page please in both languages:

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: "5. The world is interested only in what the Serbs do ... "6. Let the Muslims trample the Croats near Vitez, Busovaca, Gornji Vakuf, and Kiseljak and Kresevo. "7. Work out the operation and define the strength of the forces. " And: "8. General Perisic will give everything that does not jeopardize BG for combat readiness of units here." Sir, were you aware that Slobodan Milosevic was involved in this kind of discussion about an operation in Sarajevo with the Bosnian Serb leaders at the time of your meeting with Lord Owen in December of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And is this kind of meeting and this kind of discussion consistent with the picture that Milosevic paint for you of his relationship with the Bosnian Serb leaders at the time you arrived in Belgrade in March 1994?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't meet Milosevic on my own, i.e., without a foreign office minister or one of the international negotiators until around December of that year. So the line that would be taken in international -- in meetings with international negotiators or delegations was perforce a very one that was effective for public consumption and certainly wouldn't have the sort of language that Mladic is recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I guess the question I am trying to get at is it seems to me - and correct me if I'm wrong - that in your statement you paint a picture of what you believe the relationship between Milosevic, on the one hand, and the Bosnian Serbs, on the other hand, was at the time you arrived in Belgrade in March 1994, and that is that it was a strained relationship and that it had been a strained relationship since, let's say, May of 1993 when the Bosnian Serbs rejected the contact group plan. Can you tell me, first, am I understanding your evidence correctly? Are you indicating that in your view that was a strained relationship at the time you arrived in March of 1994?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: It was certainly strained by the late summer of that year. As for earlier, it was very hard to say. There is no specific indications. But by the late summer, the contact group were actively trying to encourage Milosevic, as indeed were Owen and Stoltenberg, in encouraging Milosevic to formally to break with the Bosnian Serbs, which is what eventually happened as we discussed earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just ask this: Are you surprised to see a record of a meeting of this kind happening in December of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: December 1993, not particularly. But I certainly would have been if it had been December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if we -- a bit further down the page we see the words, "Approved 30 T-34 tanks, ZIS field gun, shells for ZIS and B-1." Then getting close to the bottom of the page we see what appears to be Mladic's suggestion for how to proceed with the discussions where it says: "My draft conclusion. "Let us define forces, weapons, and time tomorrow, as well as the team that will decide." Then immediately after that, Milosevic says: "I agree with General Mladic's proposal ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could have the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And there it says: "But we should start the operation if the agreement is not signed and if sanctions are not lifted. "The operation is to be planned, prepared, and forces are to be concentrated, but it should not be started until we hear the results of the negotiations from Brussels." Are you able to tell us what negotiations in Brussels Milosevic is referring to here?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: These Geneva Conventions -- in Brussels? In Brussels? That surprises me. I would have thought they would have been in Geneva. I don't know what negotiation in Brussels he would have been referring to because most of the meetings with Bosnian Serbs on accepting peace plans were held in Geneva. I can't think of what results of negotiations in Brussels are, unless he is talking about internal European Union negotiations. This is a particular moment of --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Well, does --

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Where sanctions are being discussed again. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Does it assist if I indicate that apparently on the 10th and 11th of December, 1993, the European Council met in Brussels for the first time following the entry into force of the treaty on European Union. One of the things they did was to adopt a declaration on the former Yugoslavia, which, among other things, invited the Serb, Bosnian, and Croat leaders to in Brussels on 22nd December. Does that --

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, well, thank you. Had you mentioned that to start with we could have saved some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are you at all surprised -- our position is that this document shows that Milosevic is conditioning the -- or what he's saying is that an operation around Sarajevo may be conditioned on the results of negotiations in Brussels. Does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: I mean, it's hard to be surprised by Milosevic. He was a constant master of tactics and surprises. In that sense, most of them turned out to be strategic flawed, but that wouldn't stop him thinking of some tactical ploy which he thought might be helpful. It's hard to put all this in context without my having been there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. I'd now like to turn to the reasons that Mr. Milosevic supported the various peace plans. And I'd like to start just by telling you the Prosecution's position regarding the reasons for his support. We say that his support for the peace plans was not based on a -- was not because he was a humanitarian or had interest in reducing human suffering or because he had any regret or concern about the ethnic cleansing that had taken place in Bosnia. In fact, we say he, himself, had supported both the war and ethnic cleansing in Bosnia. We say that he supported the peace plans, at least in part, because the Serb side had enjoyed phenomenal success early in the war, and, in Milosevic's view, had achieved everything it could through war and violence. The peace plans provided an opportunity to consolidate a great portion of those gains and make them permanent. Milosevic was concerned that if the peace plans were not accepted, the Bosnian Serbs could lose everything they had gained, decreasing both their power and his. In Milosevic's view, in other words, the territory that had to be traded pursuant to the peace plans was worth less than the official recognition and guarantees of Serb rights that, in his view, were offered by the peace plans. Are you able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: In other words, you're saying, if I've got this right - and I'm just re-reading the transcript of what you helpfully read out - that he felt that he ought to bank the gains that the Bosnian Serbs had made before things went awry and he would lose what had been gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I'd -- I think if we are talking about the time when he was -- when we were -- when I arrived, when we were discussing earlier whether he -- Serbia -- that the Bosnian Serbs occupied 68 or 70 or 75 per cent of Bosnia, I don't think Milosevic agreed that that was sustainable and he knew that the international community would not agree that the Bosnian Serbs should have more than 49 per cent of Bosnia. In fact, that was a point that I regularly made to the Bosnian Serbs, and I remember Karadzic at one point saying that that was only his agreement, to 49 per cent, 49:51 per cent split was only a one-day offer, and because it hadn't been agreed -- it -- there hadn't been an agreement, it was no longer on the table. It was something that one kept coming back to in negotiation with the Bosnian Serbs. Karadzic, and Krajisnik in particular, would resolutely keep pushing that away and saying that that was no longer acceptable. Milosevic, however, did accept it, repeatedly accepted it, and in my experience from, say, late 1994 till Dayton, consistently argued this. And my impression was this was something -- this was partly what led to the split between Belgrade and Pale was that he was determined -- he accepted that 49:51 per cent was not negotiable. I mean, what constituted the 49 per cent was, of course, negotiable, but he wasn't going to fight for the Bosnian Serbs for anything over 49 per cent. He wasn't going to be supporting them politically and he certainly wasn't going to be supporting them anymore militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you've actually anticipated my next question to a certain extent. We say that the source of this disagreement was essentially that -- well, Milosevic wanted to cash out and go home, the Bosnian Serbs wanted to keep gambling, and in their view they could keep more land in the long run by rejecting the peace plans and continuing to fight. Therefore, the disagreement between Milosevic and the Bosnian Serbs was not a disagreement over the fundamental goal of maximising the territory over which they exercised permanent control, it was simply a dispute about what was possible, what was that maximum territory, and the best way to achieve that permanent control. Do you have a comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I would quote -- I can't now remember whether it was Richard Holbrooke, but it was probably, I think, Bob Fraser [phoen], who said something to the effect, and I'm paraphrasing now, that Milosevic was like a Chicago gangster who had decided that he was tired of his criminal activities and was now going to, as it were, cash in his chips and launder his money and live a quite life in Louisiana or somewhere and put his gangster days behind him. And that, I think, Fraser's caricature, if you like, was actually quite close to the mark. I think Milosevic had, as I think I said earlier, I can't remember if it was in response to you or your colleague across the courtroom, that I think he -- well, I'll leave it at that, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 1320 on the screen. And this document we are bringing up now is the minutes and a transcript of the tape recording of the Republika Srpska's National Assembly's -- sorry. So 65 ter 1320, please. I'm not sure this is the right document we are seeing on our screen. Ah, that's it. So this is the record of the 30th session of the Republika Srpska National Assembly from the 5th and 6th of May, 1993. And this is the occasion that you referred to in your statement when Milosevic went to Pale to promote the Vance-Owen plan. And if we could have the bottom of page 105 in English and in B/C/S ERN page 0215-0189, which is e-court page 76. So at the bottom of the page in English we see the name of Slobodan Milosevic, which indicates that he is about to be the speaker. And if we could go over to the next page in English, about the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'm going to read a portion beginning with the words, "But all the testimonies about the horrors of war ..." And it looks like that's about five lines down in the English version. So the quote is this: "But all the testimonies about the horrors of war, concluding with General Mladic's long presentation and the examples that he gave, all can be unified in one claim, in one assertion - that the war needs stop as soon as possible, that it needs to stop now. However, let me return to the question of today, which is not how great are the horrors of war, because this nation felt it in their chests throughout its entire history. Today's question is whether to consolidate the already achieved and then accomplish the rest of, what we call, the remaining 'open questions' in a peaceful process, or to ruin the already achieved, with huge losses. That is the real alternative and that is the real question on which this Assembly should decide. I do not believe that the Assembly should make such a tragic mistake in the interest of the people for whom it speaks. And it would not be the first time in history that someone created evil by wishing the biggest good for one's people, lacking the measure of what is possible and what is achievable and what are the ways to acquire something." Sir, it's our position that this excerpt sets out exactly the basis of the conflict between Milosevic and the Bosnian Serb leaders. It was a dispute about what was possible and what was achievable and the best way to acquire what they wanted. It had nothing to do with any moral rejection by Milosevic of the crimes and ethnic cleansing that had already taken place in Bosnia. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I certainly would agree that there is nothing humanitarian about his approach and his willingness or wish to bring the war to an end, and nor did I ever hear him express a single word of regret in private for anything that had happened. The numbers who had died were of no -- I never heard him express any concern about that at all. I think the -- the only gloss I would put on this, and given the fact that this is effectively a statement to the Bosnian Serb people, is that I think it's coming back to the original propaganda line, which I referred to in the article I wrote about a year ago, that what is -- what -- what he's effectively putting over is, We've saved you, or, You have saved yourself with our help from the threat of being, first of all, separated from Yugoslavia by Bosnian independents, which is not something that we wanted, and we've also -- you have taken sufficient territory to make sure you're not going to be overrun by the Muslim-Croat federation. That's, I think, the subtext there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could have the middle of the next page, which is 107, in English, and ERN page 0215-0190, e-court page 77, also the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll just read one more portion beginning with the words, "Don't say that the Serbs shall be unequal ..." And that's about halfway down the page in English. The quote is: "Don't say that the Serb shall be unequal. How can the Serbs be less sovereign than the Croats or than the Muslims in BiH that was conceived like this and based on such principles. According to this, 45 per cent of the land belongs to the Serbs and 30 per cent to the Muslims. The Serbs get 50 per cent more of the territory, while the Muslims are 50 per cent more numerous than the Serbs. The Croats get 20 per cent and some territory. So how, how, and where can one read in Vance-Owen's plans that the Serbs shall be less sovereign than the Croats or the Muslims." Now here we see Milosevic expressing his support for the Vance-Owen plan in explicitly national terms. He supported the peace plan because it gives Serbs essentially a good deal in terms of territorial size compared with population size. This represents, we say, not a rejection of ethnic cleansing but an affirmation that the project of ethnic cleansing has been successfully completed and a desire to make those results permanent. Are you able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Sorry, what particularly do you want me to comment on? I am not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Only if you are able to and if you wish to make a comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think -- the division that the international community came up with, 49 per cent to the Serbs and 51 for the Muslim Croats was not based on population. It was based on the territorial -- the areas of -- of respective control of territory going back to the land registers. So if Milosevic is just trying to make a virtue out of a -- out of the fact that at the end of the negotiation, that if the Pale Assembly accepts the Vance-Owen plan, they will get a substantial amount of land. But, of course, before the war broke out, they already had a substantial amount of land, and not based on population but on the fact that by and large Serbs were farmers and Muslims lived in the cities. It's just kind of as crude as that, if you like. But, of course, there is a big debate about the land registers and how up-to-date and authentic they were. But the 49:51 per cent deal was worked out with some acknowledgment of the fact that Serbs, as the rural dwellers, were always going to have more land than just the -- whatever it was, the 33 per cent of the population that they represented. I don't know whether that's helpful to what you were trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: It's helpful to have your comment. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have uploaded just the portions of this document consisting of Milosevic's speech as 65 ter 1320.1. And we would tender that portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Would you consider whether for contextualisation you would like to have more in, and we would then like to hear from you not later than this Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And the same comment we'd make about the bar table. It may well be in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1320.1 will receive number P3116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the issue of Milosevic's degree of influence with the Bosnian Serbs. Is it fair to say that Milosevic had an interest in indicating to you that he had less influence over the Bosnian Serbs than he may, in fact, have had?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: It depends who you mean by the Bosnian Serbs. What -- what he claimed at various points when I first came across him, when I started, he would claim that, as shown in Pale in 1993, he couldn't snap his fingers and get the Bosnian Serbs to comply with what he wanted. And part of his aim in that was to argue, Why am I subject to sanctions when the people who are causing the problem and are being obstructive and are out of my control are on the other side of the Drina. That was part of the argument. But at some stage - and I couldn't put an exact date on it - his position changed. I suppose it would have been in early late 1994, early 1995, to one where he arrogated to himself more influence that I think he actually had. He was constantly saying that he expected the Bosnian Serb Assembly to throw -- to overthrow Karadzic. So you had a Janus-like Approach. So I don't -- I can't agree with your characterisation because that's only one half of the Janus, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to quote something from that same piece regarding a meeting with Mladic from May of 2011. I am happy to have it on the screen, if you'd like to see it. I am happy just to read the quote to you as well. Perhaps I will read the quote and then you can tell me whether you would like to see it. The quote is this, and this is from the very beginning: "While none of the meetings I had with Serbian leaders during the Bosnian war could be described as pleasurable, some were less unpleasant than others. My only meeting with Ratko Mladic was, however, as grim and uncomfortable as it got. I was running the British embassy in Belgrade at this time, early 1995, and at a meeting with Slobodan Milosevic, had urged him to use his undoubted influence in Bosnian to rein in the Bosnian Serb army." What did you mean when you referred to Slobodan Milosevic's undoubted influence in Bosnia in early 1995?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: 1995. Well, Milosevic -- as I was saying earlier, Milosevic was keen to portray himself as -- at that time, as having influence with deputies from the Pale assembly whom he saw as a means of getting rid of Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Does your use of the word "undoubted influence" in that context indicate that you, yourself, believe that he had at least some influence in Bosnia, even in early 1995?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, but not comparable to the influence he had at the outset of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the -- some issues dealing with the hostage crisis. Could we please have D781 on the screen, which was 1D4847.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This is a package of documents received by the Stanisic Defence from the UK government. I don't know whether there is any reason to deal with this in private session now. Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no condition of confidentiality found. But, Mr. Jordash, it's a letter which was addressed to then lead council for Mr. Stanisic. Any need to deal with it confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. As far as I am aware, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could have page 5 in English. And I believe there is only an English version at the moment. So page 5, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, this is Belgrade telegram number 335. It's dated 6th June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could have the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Down at the bottom we see that it's, in fact, a cable from you. And I'd just like to read paragraph 6 which falls under the heading, "Comment": "While the release of some hostages may be imminent, it is unlikely that the Bosnian Serbs will let them all go without a struggle. This is their trump card; once played, their hand will be virtually empty." Sir, doesn't the simple fact that the Bosnian Serbs would give up their trump card at the behest of Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Stanisic indicate that the Belgrade leadership retained a significant degree of influence with the Pale leadership, even in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: I don't think it indicates that particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And why don't you think that it indicates that? I mean, presumably giving up one's trump card is something that's not done --

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I think trump card in the context of this particular saga. It wasn't the trump card of their whole position in the war. I think that's -- perhaps you're reading a more general comment into it than something that's quite a small -- it's not of small significance, but it relates to one small part of the whole Bosnian war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Earlier today, at page 40, you said -- the answer to your question -- this was in the context of getting Karadzic to resign from politics. And you said: "The answer to your question is that several of these maneuvers would have been conducted by Stanisic because that's who Milosevic used to try and execute his will in Bosnian when his own attempts had failed." Now, it seems to me that the hostage crisis would be one example of that; getting Karadzic to resign from politics might be another. Are there any other examples that you are aware of when Milosevic used Stanisic to execute his will in Bosnia when Milosevic's attempts had failed.

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: None that I can think of in my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And can we now have page 35 of the document on the screen in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now here, as you can see, we've jumped ahead to November of 1995. And this is Belgrade telegram number 772. It's obviously been heavily redacted, but we can see that the subject is "Dayton Peace Agreement, Serb Reactions." And if we could now go forward two pages, to page 37. At the bottom of the page I'll just read out paragraph 14. It says: "While that may be the formal position, I suspect that there may need to be some dirty work at the crossroads to ensure Bosnian Serb acquiescence. The split within the Banja Luka and Pale elements of the leadership will be an obvious focus of Milosevic's attention. It may well be that the cuddly Mr. Stanisic, the secret police chief, will be dispatched to Pale with his tried and tested (during the hostage crisis) mixture of death threats, blackmail, and bribery." Sir, the name of the author of this cable is redacted, but I'm assuming that it's you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: It could have been. But it could have been my deputy because he would have signed the telegram in my -- if I wasn't in town, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: All right. I -- I'd would just like to go through these items in order starting with the death threats. In paragraph 15 of your statement, you say that Milosevic told you that he had had -- that he had threatened to have Karadzic killed if the Bosnian Serbs would not release the UN hostages. And you also say that this message was delivered to Karadzic by Stanisic. Is it fair to say that Mr. Stanisic was an appropriate messenger for a death threat because he was a feared figure?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was -- that was certainly what Milosevic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Other than Milosevic, did you have any other source for viewing Stanisic as a feared figure?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Not that would stand up to your legal scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And according to Milosevic, who was it that feared Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And why did Karadzic fear Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: I have no idea, but I presume that -- well -- I think it has to be said that secret police chiefs are not normally known as particularly warm and genial figures, and certainly not in Serbia. The history of them for going back to Rankovic in Tito's time was not to one for the squeamish. So I think if you receive a call from your erstwhile patron and now somewhat strained patron as police chief who tells you that Mr. Milosevic plans to have you killed if you don't let the hostages go, you're -- you're -- it will at least focus your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Moving on to the -- the second point, blackmail. Is it also fair to say that Mr. Stanisic was someone perceived to know a great many secrets and who, therefore, might be in a position to blackmail others?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: I think one of the documents we looked at earlier said as much in the document about the splits between the Serbian security service and the Bosnian Serb security service, if I'm -- my memory serves me. One of the reasons for Karadzic and Krajisnik's unhappiness was precisely that they saw the Serbian security people meddling and able to use their knowledge of the corruption of the -- of the Bosnian Serb leadership to effectively blackmail them to comply with their -- with their, in this case -- Milosevic's wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And moving on to the third point, bribery. Are you aware of any reason that Stanisic would be in a position to -- to offer bribes or incentives to the Bosnian Serb leaders in order to get them to do what Milosevic wanted?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: It was said after the event - and again, I can't quite remember the locus - that Milosevic had supplied in contravention of his own self-imposed embargo some spare parts for the Bosnia Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: At the time of the hostage crisis?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes. In -- as a bribe to release the hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir Ivor, thank you for answering my questions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farr. Mr. Bakrac, position still the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, do you have any further questions in re-examination for the witness, and how much time would that approximately take?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I do have approximately 15 minutes of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes, which -- I'm also looking at you because we -- we started almost quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would also -- sorry to interrupt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would also like to address you for five minutes on an issue which arose during my learned friend's cross-examination. In the absence of the witness is probably wisest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then to do that before you re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could do that. I think what would be the most logical way of proceeding would be that we already give a break to the witness, that you address the Chamber during five minutes. We then take a break and resume at most likely approximately five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sir Ivor, the Stanisic Defence would like to address the Chamber in your absence, so you get the early break today. Would you please follow the usher and we will continue in a little bit over half an hour, and then it will not take very long any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I am trying to find the place in the transcript, because the -- the -- the issue is this: That it's been put quite clearly to the witness - and I will find it in the transcript shortly - but it's been put very clearly to the witness two things which are of significance -- of huge significance for the case. First of all, that ethnic transfer had been completed by, I think, 1993 or 1994. And secondly, and related to that, that Milosevic was acting to, at that point -- I want to be careful here so I don't misquote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, are you referring to page 73, lines 12 and following, where Mr. Farr in his question suggests an interpretation of the words of Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, yes, although it's not an interpretation of Mr. -- no, sorry, that was the context in which the Prosecution asked the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- but Mr. Farr clearly said "this represents, we say, affirmation that the project of ethnic cleansing had been completed." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's of huge significance because we say that ethnic cleansing had been completed and Sanski Most and Trnovo in 1995 had nothing to do with that, and the criminal enterprise, if it existed, had ended, and that seems to be consistent with what the Prosecution put to the witness. Earlier in that -- I begged your pardon. I'd hoped to have the transcript on paper, but I think there -- the point -- the ancillary point is that the Prosecution appeared to -- to accept to a significant degree the Defence position that Milosevic was, as this witness has confirmed, supporting the peace agreement, the motives behind it obviously in dispute, but that again is something which Mr. Farr made clear. And what I would respectfully ask is that the Prosecution make that position clear, to put to a witness these fundamental points which appear to agree with the Defence position ought to be made explicit, in our submission, and we ought to know at this side of the room and Your Honours ought to know whether that is the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm read reading what you said, Mr. Jordash. Now, correct me when I'm wrong. Mr. Farr, in your question you linked, although the text of the quote didn't seem to give a direct -- such a direct link - you said, Well, this whole discussion about accepting 49:51 per cent, look, isn't this a clear expression of Mr. Milosevic doing that, ethnic cleansing being completed. Whereas the quote you gave doesn't say anything about ethnic cleansing. It was -- you introduced that. And as a matter of fact, I noticed, not only now, but already at the time, that whatever the witness said about ambition of getting more or less or -- but he left the whole ethnic cleansing out of his answer, so to that extent I do not find him to confirm in any way the direct link, as you suggested, with the ethnic cleansing. Let me first try to verify whether this is a -- an accurate understanding of both your question and the answer, and I'm looking both to you, Mr. Farr, and to you as well, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now -- Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was putting our -- putting our case to the witness, but I -- I think what this highlights is -- the purpose of putting the case to the witness is so that the witness is not confused. It's not a way for the Prosecution to amend its pleadings by sloppy wording. And I didn't intend to do that. Of course, we continue to rely on the indictment. We rely on the pre-trial brief. My goal was to make sure that if the witness had something that he wanted to say about that, that would be useful for the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber would have an opportunity to hear that. Of course, it's not our case that the criminal plan ended in May 1993. That's clear from the indictment. We say it lasted until December of 1995. Your Honour, may I confer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I think -- the one thing that I think I can say is that we don't contest Milosevic's support for the peace plans. What's disputed about that is the motivation for it, and in particular the Defence argument set out in the pre-trial brief -- in their pre-trial brief at paragraph 245 and 249 that Stanisic's support for these peace plans somehow demonstrate that he could not have the criminal intent required for the JCE. In other words, their case is that support for the peace plan necessarily means that one -- never in one's life intended the forcible permanent removal of non-Serbs from large portions of Bosnia Croatia. Our case on that point is that if one's support for peace plans is designed to lock in the degree of ethnic cleansing that has already bene achieved and has already been completed, then it does no such thing. In fact, it tends to make the opposite point, that, in fact, it demonstrates a desire to consolidate those results. Again, to say that it was completed at that point was sloppy wording, and wasn't intended as a modification of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I would ask you the following. You may comment on what Mr. Farr said. If you say, Well, his answer doesn't satisfy me, then tell us in very practical terms what you expect Mr. Farr to tell the witness? Try to phrase, help him, assist him, in what he should put to the witness so that I fully understand what you think is missing in the way in which the Prosecution presents it case to the witness. Apart from I am not at this moment yet anticipating on any duty -- I'd first like to know from you that you say what you should put to the witness, A, B or c, because that apparently -- and then we have two matters. First, whether that is the position of the Prosecution, and we had a bit of a discussion about what exactly their position is. And the second is to what extent they are under an obligation to put it in that kind of terms to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Unlike our usual submissions, in some senses I am not suggesting that my learned friend should have put any particular thing to the witness. I'm -- I'm submitting that my learned friend should not have put something to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- if that is not part of their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the completion of the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That is, as I understand the Prosecution case, the ethnic cleansing continue through 1995. And that -- the pursuit -- that's the criminal object which was being pursued until 1995, I understood because it hasn't been qualified any differently it's best that -- that actually meant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then stop you there for one second. Talking about whether or not the ethnic cleansing was completed, yes or no. The witness in his answer more or less ignored it. Would Mr. Farr then have to repeat it again and say, But I told you -- or is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, because the witness hasn't -- I didn't seek to elicit from the witness the factual situation on the ground, whether ethnic cleansing had been completed by 1995 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether it was a misleading presentation of the Prosecution's position, it has had no effect because the witness didn't even touch upon it, unless you say that's the bad result of misrepresenting your own case, but I didn't gain that impression. But am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree. I'm not suggesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- that anything fresh should be put to the witness. I am just making an inquiry of the Prosecution, if you like, through Your Honours, if -- because if that's the -- I wanted to know the answer to the question because I wanted to be sure when re-examining the witness that I'm doing so on [overlapping speakers] basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proper understanding of the Prosecution's case. Anything else at this moment you would suggest, or do you say with these answers I can continue after the break? Because that's my --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I -- I am not sure I understand the Prosecution's position entirely. I am not sure that it's clear whether they do say the ethnic cleansing was completed or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- I did understand it. But please correct me when I'm wrong, Mr. Farr, that I would say, consolidating your position, that you would consider that not to be without a link to the ethnic cleansing which was performed until then? Is that a right understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I am not sure I understood what Your Honour was saying just then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if ethnic cleansing is complete, that means it's done, nothing has to be done anymore if you want to ethnically cleanse an area. I did understand where you linked the speech of Mr. Milosevic to the ethnic cleansing being completed, that you intended to say that, well, taking advantage of the ethnic cleansing to the extent it has taken place already. Is that your --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, that is how I understand it and that's how apparently Mr. Farr intended it, although not very neatly formulated. Is this sufficient for you to consider after the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, in some ways it's not. I -- I don't want to be difficult, but if there is -- and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal suggests that there had been ethnic cleansing and it occurred and continued and had pretty much been completed by 1992. I'm referring, for example, to the Krajisnik judgement, they're not -- the further one gets away from the actual ethnic cleansing, the less the Prosecution's submission has weight. What I mean by that is if Mr. Stanisic is supporting a peace plan in the beginning of 1993, one can easily say, Well, how could that possibly impact upon or remove the inference that he intended forcible displacement one month before. It's clear that the Prosecution's submission would have more weight, that Mr. Stanisic could be said to be trying to consolidate those gains. When one moves then to 1995, the inference that one can draw - that the Prosecution will seek to have you draw - gets, I think, less and less strong. And that's why it's important to us to know whether the Prosecution accept that the majority of the ethnic cleansing had been completed by 1992 or 1993. Things that happen in 1995 are significantly some distance away from that -- those actual factual events on the ground. We will say that the further one gets away, the less one can infer criminal intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I would say is that neither the Defence nor the Court should ever assume that we have attempted to modify our indictment by a badly written question that was written late at night. And again, just to return, the purpose of putting the case is to make sure that the witness is not confused. I think that the question served that purse. It certainly wasn't intended to do anything with respect to the charges. It wasn't intended to change the allegation in the indictment, and we would just say that if we intend to do that we will make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meaning that the forcible removal was still on the agenda apart from what the position was during these peace negotiations and apart from the extent to which it had already been achieved or was still to be achieved?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Correct. Until the end of the -- end of the alleged joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers that the matter has been sufficiently clarified by the Prosecution for the Defence to be able to re-examine the witness after the break, and we'll have a break until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, are you ready to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just have very questions left, Sir Ivor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please, could we have on the screen P2358.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We return to the Supreme Defence Council minutes. You were asked questions by my learned friend from the Prosecution about Mr. Milosevic's motivations, and I just want to clarify some issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have please page 39 of the -- sorry, no, page 48 of the English and 32 of the B/C/S. And this is a continuation of a speech by Milosevic that we looked at earlier. It should be P2358.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. So we should have page 48 of the English and 32 of the B/C/S. And the section I am interested in is the last paragraph, where Milosevic says: "This nation shall not be slaughtered because of the three hot heads from Pale. And our towns full of young people shall no be bombed because someone wishes to take more than half of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina since one half is not sufficient, even though they don't have a enough population to inhabitant it." And then over the page, please, to page 49 of the English and 33 of the B/C/S: "As for our domestic public, it is for peace. Seselj does not represent the domestic public. And mark my words, the opposition's paramilitary formations have gone down the drain a long time ago. They are just a small and pathetic bunch that doesn't have nickels to rub together. The army should not be concerned with their paramilitary formations. The police here are quite capable of dealing with them, wherever they dare to show their face. "The second great danger that we had faced was the introduction of more severe sanctions. As I said, the first danger was the drawing of Yugoslavia into the war."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: As we can see, Sir Ivor, there is a number of concerns Milosevic expresses. Does this or not reflect the type of conversations you were having with Milosevic concerning his concerns?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, they would be broadly in line with these sort of concerns he would be expressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the reference to the opposition's paramilitary formations. Are you able to offer any insight into what Milosevic was concerned about there?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: I think he is talking about people like -- about Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Seselj's impact where?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: In paramilitaries in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then if we can turn, please, to 1D3612. Again Supreme Defence Council minutes, this time held on the 2nd of November, 1994. I think this should be under seal too, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. I am confused with the transcript. Is it 1D3612, I see indicated in the transcript? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D -- yeah. This document is not e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Actually, I am happy to leave that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just finish then, Sir Ivor, if I may, with a couple of other questions. First of all, was there a provision in the Dayton peace agreement concerning refugees or displaced people?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure there was. I can't remember the details now, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can deal with that then by tendering at a later stage the Dayton peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or agree on the matter, Mr. Jordash. I take it that the content of the Dayton peace agreement could -- well, I would be optimistic to expect the parties to agree on that. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope it's not over optimistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that might be one thing we could agree on, but I won't detain Sir Ivor with that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You left with region when, Sir Ivor?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: I formally left in the beginning of November 1997, and I subsequently went back as the foreign secretary's secret representative on two occasions in 1998. This was when Mr. Robin Cook was the British foreign secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you back in 1998, do you know if Mr. Stanisic was still in the position of chief of state security?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: I believe so. But I would think you would know better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I am not sure anybody is interested in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you agree with the Prosecution, everyone would be happy, Mr. Jordash. It's, again, seems not to be a matter which is really in dispute, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I was leading to the next question, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then put that next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- whether the witness is aware of Mr. Stanisic leaving his position at that time and the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, neither of my two visits which were entirely focused on Kosovo was there ever any mention of Mr. Stanisic that I can recall in my long meetings which took place in I think March and July, from memory, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you meet Milosevic during those?

utterances.speaker: SIR IVOR ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the purpose of my visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May just have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir Ivor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH

utterances.text: Yes. And then we can add two MFIs to our list for this Wednesday and hope to resolve it on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, apparently no observations on behalf of the Stanisic Defence. 1D05453, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.text: Then the status remains as it was before. Mr. Jordash, have you prepared a 92 summary for this witness.

utterances.text: Yes. And there are a couple of other things, if I may, with the exhibit.

utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then we first deal with the exhibits.

utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could you repeat the number, whether document ID or the number assigned to it for the one you said is now part of a -- was already part of your -- was that P3116, document 65 ter 1320.1?

utterances.text: .1, which appears to be P3115. The suggestion would then be, Mr. Farr, to vacate the excerpt found in 65 ter 1345.1 and then to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, one potential concern is that that may affect the references in the witness testimony where I am referring to particular pages of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: It was only a three- or four-page excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was only three or four pages -- actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'm mindful that it could result in some duplication, but I think it would be perhaps a smaller burden than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it's more practical to leave it as it is, even if we have a couple of pages as a double in the system, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Nope, that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you have prepared a 92 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please read it into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sir Ivor Roberts entered the diplomatic service in 1968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when reading, could you already slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. And until his requirement in 2006 was posted to serve in various positions in London, Lebanon, Paris, Canberra, Vanuatu, Madrid, Belgrade, Dublin, and Rome. In Belgrade, the witness served as British charges d'affaires, then ambassador. In this role, he had the opportunity to meet often with Slobodan Milosevic 40 to 50 times over nearly four years. At the time the witness arrived to the FRY in early 1994, Milosevic was still smarting 6 c from the Bosnian Serb's rejection of the Vance-Owen plan. It was the witness's opinion that Milosevic worked to bring the Bosnian Serbs under control. After various fruitless attempts to get the Bosnian Serbs to accept the contact group's plan, Milosevic lost patience with the Pale leadership, and reacting from pressure from the international negotiators, Lord Owen and Thorvald Stoltenberg, he ordered the closure of the border between the FRY and Bosnia. The witness further mentioned that Lord Owen had a complex relationship with Milosevic. He and the witness believed that Milosevic, since accepting the Vance-Owen peace plan, had been engaged in a policy of trying to bring the war in Bosnia to a close and that he was actively looking for a solution to the problems. In his statement the witness notes that Milosevic and Karadzic did not have a good relationship during his time in Belgrade. Milosevic was humiliated in Pale in 1993 when he tried, unsuccessfully, to persuade the Bosnian Serbs to agree to the Vance-Owen peace plan. The witness notes that he regard Karadzic as a major stumbling block to his efforts to bring the war in Bosnia to an end, and Milosevic was trying force him from office. The witness also discusses the UN hostage crisis in his statement. When the witness learned about this matter, he immediately went to see Milosevic and impressed upon him how much he needed the British soldiers out in one piece. Milosevic assured him that he would do what he could do get them released. Later, Milosevic told the witness that he was sending Stanisic to Bosnia to see Karadzic about resolving the hostage crisis. The witness also describes his own experience during the hostage crisis and the contributions he made to its resolution. Throughout the UN hostage crisis, the witness had no meetings with Stanisic; although, his deputy met him once at a briefing he gave. More generally, the witness has only met Mr. Stanisic once. This meeting involved no more than a handshake and took place in November/December 1995 at the Belgrade military airport Batajnica. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. I'd like to briefly go into private session.

utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Marcus, please proceed. We are discussing at this moment proposals for more efficient housekeeping session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. We responded on Friday, we've since then inputted into this chart as well the Defence's position. But it's quite substantial, Your Honours. It's about 100 pages of issues. But in our -- in the Prosecution's submission, a lot of these issues have been discussed previously, the positions of the parties have already been put on the record numerous times, and it's our view that if this -- if the Defence can either confirm what we've put in there, we've -- if the Defence have put their position, it's in the chart, if they have additional points, they can add it into the chart. It's very similar to our bar table procedure. So we left that -- we took that model. And then, Your Honours, our submission is that we would only need to discuss on Wednesday any additional matters for which we haven't already made submissions. So for these matters which are still pending from the 24th November housekeeping or from the 12th December submission that the Prosecution made, all of those matters can be, in our view, dealt with in correspondence, with the Chamber's leave, before -- before Wednesday, and Wednesday could simply be used for the Chamber to -- to put those -- its -- its decisions on the record, for I would say maybe two-thirds or even three quarters of the issues on the chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hs the Chamber -- has the Chamber been provided with a copy of the chart --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with your comments. Then I'm a bit -- well, perhaps I'm not totally surprised that they haven't seen it because -- for all kind of reasons. Is the Defence comment already in it or is there a new copy to be expected with the Defence comments in it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We have not received any response from the Defence. What we have done is for those issues, which they raised in their filing, we have noted that in our copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- because we offered to tender the joint position -- to provide it, not tender it maybe, but to provide it to the Chamber afterwards. So we have running version that we've kept. We've inputted what they've said in their submissions, but that only covered maybe 15 or 20 of the documents and the rest are all remaining there. This is just are a proposal, Your Honours, to save us court time. I don't think it's really necessary to go through it on the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, whatever the final outcome will be, is the Defence willing to prepare the housekeeping session on the basis of the chart prepared by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I feel a bit hurt that we haven't been asked if we have done our homework, and we are doing our homework. It's just a 98-page document and we are finalising it, and we will have it filled in by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have a common experience what it takes to go through MFI lists. That is true for the parties but for the Bench as well. When do you think it could be ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it should be ready by the end of tomorrow. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would leave me the night to further prepare --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Homework for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. No, I'm just establishing the practical consequences. If you -- if you have -- would have done half the work, would you be willing already to share the half of that work with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, what I will do is if I've -- what I've just been told is it's coming to me by early tomorrow morning, so I will undertake to get it to everybody by lunch, if that's satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would certainly assist, and we'll include this in our preparations for the housekeeping session. Ms. Marcus, did you ever have such a quick success in your initiatives?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Yes, yes. I don't expect a serious answer to that. Then we adjourn for the day and we resume Wednesday, the 28th of March, at 9.00 in the morning, in this same Courtroom II where a housekeeping session will be held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.48 p.m.,
